  "title": "MathPrism: Cross-Modal IRT-Guided Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Visual Mathematical Reasoning",
  "core_problem": "Current methods for improving VLM mathematical reasoning have made rapid progress on modality-aware reward decomposition (MoCA, PDCR, Perception-R1, Vision-SR1, PRCO, CogFlow, PEARL — all 2025–2026) and capability-staged training ('From Seeing to Thinking,' RuCL, Infi-MMR), yet they all share a critical blind spot: difficulty scheduling and data selection remain heuristic. MoCA routes rewards to 'bad seeing' vs 'bad thinking' but trains on a fixed dataset with no curriculum. CogFlow (ICLR 2026) decomposes training into perception→internalization→reasoning stages with Visual-Gated Policy Optimization but uses fixed quality thresholds with no difficulty progression. PEARL (CVPR 2026) conditions reasoning updates on perception checklist gates but uses binary pass/fail with no difficulty-aware scheduling. 'From Seeing to Thinking' stages by capability type (perception→reasoning) but uses no difficulty progression within stages. Infi-MMR phases training from text to caption-augmented to multimodal but uses predetermined phases rather than data-driven scheduling. MathForge (ICLR 2026) introduces difficulty-aware GRPO (DGPO) with MAD-based advantage normalization but uses empirical accuracy as a coarse scalar difficulty proxy in text-only settings. VideoCuRL (Dec 2025) makes the closest advance: it decomposes video difficulty into two orthogonal axes — Visual-Temporal Perception Load (optical flow, keyframe entropy) and Cognitive Reasoning Depth (Calibrated Surprisal) — with a competence-aware Diagonal Wavefront curriculum scheduler. This demonstrates the value of multi-dimensional difficulty decomposition for RL training, but relies on training-free heuristic proxies that the authors acknowledge 'may under-represent the difficulty of visually subtle yet semantically dense scenes' and that produce high within-bin performance variance. PUDF and RIDE pioneer IRT-guided curriculum learning and IRT-based RL reward, respectively, but operate in text-only settings with 1PL models that treat difficulty as a single scalar — missing the multimodal decomposition entirely. M3IRT (Mar 2026) demonstrated across 24 VLMs on three benchmarks that VLM ability and item difficulty decompose into distinct modality-specific components (θ_base, θ_img, θ_txt, θ_cross), revealing that many top-performing models rely on text shortcuts rather than genuine cross-modal integration. This diagnostic power has never been connected to training: no existing method uses cross-modal IRT decomposition to decide WHICH problems to train on, at WHAT difficulty, targeting WHICH modality weakness. The result: even models trained with modality-aware rewards or staged pipelines develop lopsided ability profiles because the training data itself was not selected to address diagnosed weaknesses — the reward tells the model HOW to learn but not WHAT to learn next.",
  "opportunity": "Six independently mature threads can now be unified: (1) Cross-modal IRT decomposition (M3IRT, Mar 2026) is technically feasible and diagnostically powerful — decomposing both VLM ability and item difficulty into modality-specific components via multidimensional 2PL IRT. (2) Modality-decomposed rewards have reached maturity at top venues — MoCA (ICML 2026 Spotlight) provides blindfolded reasoning for perception verification, PDCR (CVPR 2026) introduces visual dependence scores, Perception-R1 (ICLR 2026) demonstrates visual perception reward effectiveness with only 1,442 samples, CogFlow (ICLR 2026) introduces Synergistic Visual Rewards (VPR+VSR) with Visual-Gated Policy Optimization, and PEARL (CVPR 2026) uses perception checklists as fidelity gates (+9.7% over baseline, +6.6% over GRPO on MathVerse). (3) Multi-dimensional difficulty-aware curriculum RL has been demonstrated: VideoCuRL (Dec 2025) decomposes video difficulty into orthogonal perception and reasoning axes with Diagonal Wavefront scheduling, proving multi-axis curricula outperform single-axis ones (−1.5% to −3.1% when either axis is ablated), but relies on heuristic proxies. In the text-only domain, MathForge (ICLR 2026) shows difficulty-aware advantage normalization (DGPO) improves RL (+4.56% over GRPO) but uses scalar empirical accuracy; AdaRFT provides adaptive reward-based difficulty scheduling with 2× speedup; GRPO-LEAD (EMNLP 2025) adds difficulty-aware advantage reweighting. All use empirical proxies rather than principled psychometric difficulty estimation. (4) Procedural visual math generation is established at scale (DynaMath, MAVIS, SDE-GPG) and SynthRL (Jun 2025) demonstrates LLM-based difficulty augmentation for visual reasoning RL with verifiable rewards, but none connect generation to modality-specific IRT difficulty targeting. (5) Capability-staged training for VLMs has matured (VL-Cogito, Curr-ReFT, Infi-MMR, 'From Seeing to Thinking'), with complementary perception RL methods (ViCrit's verifiable perception proxy task, V-Triune/Orsta's unified reasoning+perception RL). (6) Hierarchical Bayesian IRT estimation enables stable parameter estimation even with small calibration panels (N=50 with OH2PL), and PUDF's Artificial Crowds technique (13 models × 5 checkpoints = 60+ respondents) demonstrates practical scalability. The untapped synthesis: use M3IRT's multimodal 2PL cross-modal profiles to DIAGNOSE modality-specific weaknesses (what to improve), adopt proven modality-decomposed rewards to OPTIMIZE learning signals (how to improve), use IRT-parameterized generators to PRODUCE targeted training data (what to train on), and SCHEDULE training via Fisher-information-guided multi-dimensional curriculum with confidence-aware fallback (when to increase difficulty along each modality axis). VideoCuRL demonstrates that orthogonal difficulty decomposition improves curriculum RL; MathPrism provides the IRT-grounded instantiation with formal uncertainty quantification, integrated data generation, and reward calibration — closing the loop between psychometric evaluation and training that PUDF makes for text-only 1PL but no work makes for cross-modal multimodal settings. MathLens independently validates our premise: RL and SFT target different capability components, and remaining errors increasingly stem from multimodal-specific integration failures that require targeted intervention.",
  "landscape": "**IRT for LLM evaluation and training:** M3IRT (arXiv:2603.02663, Mar 2026) decomposes VLM ability and item difficulty into base, image, text, and cross-modal components via multidimensional 2PL IRT across 24 VLMs, revealing text shortcut reliance — evaluation-only. PUDF (arXiv:2408.05326, Computational Linguistics) uses 1PL IRT with Artificial Crowds (13 models × 5 epoch checkpoints = 60 effective respondents) for curriculum learning via DDS-MAE (Dynamic Data Selection via Model Ability Estimation), re-estimating model ability each epoch with MLE and incrementally adjusting when stagnant — text-only, no modality decomposition, no RL. RIDE (arXiv:2511.04120, Jan 2026) trains a difficulty ranker on 1PL IRT estimations from 35 LLMs and uses it as RL reward for adversarial question rewriting, causing 21.73% average performance drop across 26 models — text-only, uses IRT for difficulty reward not curriculum scheduling. ATLAS (arXiv:2511.04689, Nov 2025) applies 3PL IRT with Fisher-information-guided adaptive item selection achieving 90% evaluation reduction — text-only, evaluation-only. Growing Pains (arXiv:2604.12843, Apr 2026) uses multidimensional IRT with anchor items for extensible benchmarking — text-only, evaluation-only. Gap: PUDF and RIDE prove IRT can guide training, but only in text-only 1PL settings; no work uses cross-modal multidimensional 2PL IRT to guide multimodal training curriculum or data generation.

**Modality-decomposed rewards in VLM RL:** MoCA / 'Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking' (arXiv:2605.14054, ICML 2026 Spotlight) introduces Modality-Aware Credit Assignment using a blindfolded text reasoner (Qwen2.5-14B) as perception verifier, with gating logic that protects correct-perception tokens from negative gradients when downstream reasoning fails; achieves +15.2 on V*, +5.6 on MathVista. PDCR (arXiv:2605.13467, CVPR 2026) computes Visual Dependence Scores via log-likelihood ratios (real vs. blank image) and uses Otsu's method for unsupervised perception/reasoning step clustering with intra-cluster normalization. Perception-R1 (arXiv:2506.07218, ICLR 2026) introduces visual perception reward via annotation matching, achieving SOTA with only 1,442 training samples. CogFlow (arXiv:2601.01874, ICLR 2026) implements a three-stage perception→internalization→reasoning framework with Synergistic Visual Rewards (combining Visual Parameterized Reward using parametric equations + Hungarian matching for geometric fidelity, and Visual Semantic Reward using FG-CLIP for perceptual coherence), Knowledge Internalization Reward (Softmax-DPO with 1:5 pos/neg trajectory pairs bridging perception and reasoning), and Visual-Gated Policy Optimization (VGPO-CogFlow: quality-based filtering accepting perception trajectories above threshold τ before reasoning); MathCog dataset provides 120K+ perception-reasoning aligned annotations; achieves MathVista 76.8%, MathVerse 53.9%, DynaMath 46.2% on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Note: CogFlow's 'VGPO' (Visual-Gated Policy Optimization) shares its acronym with VGPO by Wan et al. (arXiv:2604.09349, Visually-Guided Policy Optimization); both address visual faithfulness but via different mechanisms — quality threshold gating vs. attention compensation and dual-grained advantage re-weighting. PEARL (arXiv:2511.18437, CVPR 2026) introduces Perceptual-Evidence Anchored Reinforced Learning using perception checklists — auto-generated sub-questions with verifiable answers probing visual understanding — as a fidelity gate for reasoning; dual rewards (perceptual + reasoning) with conditional policy updates only if perception checks pass; +9.7% over baseline, +6.6% over GRPO on MathVerse; integrates with GRPO/DAPO. Vision-SR1 (arXiv:2508.19652, Aug 2025) implements self-rewarding VLM via reasoning decomposition with decoupled reward-advantage framework for visual vs language rewards. PRCO / 'Seeing with You' (arXiv:2603.28618, Mar 2026) introduces dual-role Observer-Solver RLVR with role-specific rewards: Observer receives utility reward from Solver's downstream success, reducing perception errors by 39.2%. AT-RL / 'Credit Where It is Due' (arXiv:2602.11455, Feb 2026) identifies cross-modal anchor tokens (~15% of tokens) via attention topology and selectively reinforces them, with 32B model surpassing 72B baseline on MathVista (80.2%). VGPO-Wan / Visually-Guided Policy Optimization (arXiv:2604.09349, ACL 2026, hereafter VGPO-Wan to distinguish from CogFlow's Visual-Gated variant) introduces visual attention compensation and dual-grained advantage re-weighting to combat temporal visual forgetting during reasoning. Perceval (arXiv:2604.24583, Apr 2026) provides perception-centric process reward models with token-level error grounding via claim-by-claim visual evidence comparison. ViCrit (arXiv:2506.10128, Jun 2025) introduces a verifiable RL proxy task where VLMs learn to detect synthetic hallucinations in image captions with binary exact-match rewards; improvements transfer to visual math reasoning, demonstrating perception RL benefits but without curriculum or IRT integration. V-Triune/Orsta (arXiv:2505.18129, May 2025) unifies RL for reasoning, perception, and localization via Sample-Level Reward Routing, Verifier-Level Outcome Verification, and Dynamic IoU reward shaping at 7B–32B scale; matches specialist mixtures under comparable compute but without difficulty-aware scheduling. None use IRT for reward calibration or curriculum-aware data selection.

**Capability-staged and curriculum RL for VLMs:** VideoCuRL (arXiv:2601.00887, Dec 2025) is the closest conceptual parallel to our multi-dimensional difficulty curriculum: it decomposes video difficulty into two orthogonal axes — Visual-Temporal Perception Load (quantified via optical flow magnitude and keyframe entropy as training-free heuristic proxies) and Cognitive Reasoning Depth (quantified via Calibrated Surprisal, the information gain of text answers beyond a language prior) — mapping data onto a K×K grid (K=4). A competence-aware Diagonal Wavefront scheduler advances training from easy-easy (B_{0,0}) to hard-hard (B_{K-1,K-1}) using a Local Competence Score (exponential moving average of rewards in each bucket) gated by threshold T; neighboring harder buckets activate only when competence exceeds T. Ablations confirm both axes are necessary: visual-only scheduling drops −1.5% on VSI-Bench, cognitive-only drops −3.1% on MVBench. Achieves +2.5% VideoMME, +2.7% VSI-Bench on Qwen2.5-VL-7B with Video-R1-260k dataset. Key limitations acknowledged by the authors: heuristic proxies 'may under-represent the difficulty of visually subtle yet semantically dense scenes' and serve as 'probabilistic guides rather than deterministic labels,' with high within-bin performance variance indicating coarse difficulty estimation. VideoCuRL targets video understanding (not visual math), has no data generation component, no reward calibration, and no formal uncertainty quantification for difficulty estimates. MathPrism differs fundamentally: (a) psychometric IRT provides calibrated, continuous difficulty profiles with formal uncertainty (posterior variance) vs. VideoCuRL's heuristic proxies that lack confidence bounds; (b) IRT decomposition enables targeted data generation (Component 2) — VideoCuRL only selects from existing data; (c) IRT-calibrated reward weighting λ(θ) dynamically adjusts perception vs. reasoning emphasis — VideoCuRL modifies only scheduling, not reward structure; (d) confidence-aware fallback ensures graceful degradation when estimates are unreliable. VideoCuRL validates the premise that orthogonal difficulty decomposition improves curriculum RL; MathPrism provides the IRT-grounded instantiation with generation and reward calibration for visual math.

'From Seeing to Thinking' (arXiv:2605.20177, ICML 2026) decomposes post-training into perception → textual reasoning → visual reasoning with GRPO, showing +5.2% on WeMath with 20.8% shorter chains; critically claims 'capability-based staging is orthogonal to difficulty-based curricula' and shows combining both dimensions yields best results (62.99% vs 60.53% staging-only vs 60.36% difficulty-only). VL-Cogito (arXiv:2507.22607, Jul 2025) applies PCuRL with online difficulty soft weighting across easy/medium/hard stages and dynamic length reward. Curr-ReFT (arXiv:2503.07065, Mar 2025) stages training from visual perception to complex reasoning. E2H Reasoner (arXiv:2506.06632, Jun 2025) provides convergence guarantees for easy-to-hard curriculum RL. Observe-R1 (arXiv:2505.12432, May 2025) introduces dynamic progressive RL with NeuraLadder (+3.2% MathVista). RuCL (arXiv:2602.21628, Feb 2026) reformulates curriculum as reward design, stratifying rubrics from perception to logical reasoning with dynamic weight adjustment (+7.83% over Qwen2.5-VL-7B). VCRL (arXiv:2509.19803, Sep 2025) uses reward variance as difficulty proxy. Infi-MMR (arXiv:2505.23091, May 2025) implements curriculum-phased RL for multimodal small language models through three phases — foundational reasoning activation (text-only RL), cross-modal reasoning adaptation (caption-augmented multimodal), multimodal reasoning enhancement (caption-free) — achieving 67.2% MathVista testmini and 43.68% MathVerse at 3B scale; demonstrates that curriculum phasing from text to multimodal is effective but uses predetermined phases without IRT-based scheduling. MathForge (arXiv:2601.20614, ICLR 2026) proposes Difficulty-Aware GRPO (DGPO) replacing standard deviation normalization with Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD) for difficulty-balanced group advantage estimation, where difficulty is negative mean accuracy; also introduces Multi-Aspect Question Reformulation (MQR) generating background/term/sub-problem variants for difficulty-controllable augmentation; text-only on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, averaging +4.56% over GRPO. AdaRFT (arXiv:2504.05520, Apr 2025) introduces adaptive curriculum reinforcement fine-tuning that dynamically adjusts problem difficulty based on recent reward signals, maintaining an optimal challenge level where tasks are challenging but solvable; achieves 2× training time reduction on competition-level math (AMC/AIME/IMO-style); text-only, lightweight extension to standard PPO without modifying reward function; uses reward-based difficulty estimation, not IRT profiles. GRPO-LEAD (arXiv:2504.09696, EMNLP 2025) adds difficulty-aware advantage reweighting for concise mathematical reasoning at 14B scale; text-only. SPEED-RL (arXiv:2506.09016, Jun 2025; withdrawn) establishes theoretically that intermediate-difficulty prompts improve the gradient estimator's signal-to-noise ratio, accelerating RL convergence 2–6×; the theoretical insight supports our Fisher-information-based selection rationale, though our approach derives difficulty from IRT rather than empirical accuracy. 'Unlocking Difficulty Prior' (arXiv:2505.13261, May 2025) applies difficulty priors in data curation (U-shaped filtering), advantage reweighting, and difficulty-aware prompts using empirical accuracy as proxy. All use heuristic difficulty measures; none employ IRT difficulty decomposition.

**Diagnostic-driven training:** DPE (arXiv:2602.22859, Feb 2026) proposes spiral diagnostic-training loops with multi-agent weakness annotation and targeted data generation — diagnoses at coarse category level without psychometric grounding. DPPO (arXiv:2511.16602, Nov 2025) implements Deliberate Practice PO with a metacognitive metaloop alternating RL diagnosis and SFT remediation; reports +20.3% on Pelican-VL 1.0 (their own embodied VLM built on Qwen2.5-VL base, 7B–72B scale), targeting embodied intelligence tasks rather than mathematical reasoning; the metacognitive loop concept (diagnose→improve) is conceptually related but operates in a different domain with different evaluation criteria. Error-driven LMM tuning (arXiv:2412.15652, Dec 2024) uses teacher models to identify capability gaps (+7%) — retrieves rather than generates. Critic-V (CVPR 2025) uses Actor-Critic for inference-time refinement.

**Visual math data generation:** DynaMath (ICLR 2025) implements 501 seed programs across 9 math topics. DynaSolidGeo (arXiv:2510.22340, Oct 2025) extends to solid geometry (503 seeds). MAVIS (ICLR 2025) produces 834K visual math problems — generates without modality-aware difficulty control. SynthRL (arXiv:2506.02096, Jun 2025) introduces a scalable pipeline for visual reasoning data synthesis: an LLM synthesizer (Gemini-2.5-Flash) rewrites visual math questions into harder variants while preserving answers, with two-criterion verification (correctness: ≥4/16 rollouts pass on target model; difficulty: pass count decreases by ≥2); applied to MMK12 (8K seeds → 3.3K synthesized), yielding +1.0% average across 5 visual math benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B; treats difficulty holistically without modality-specific decomposition or IRT parameterization. SDE-GPG (arXiv:2506.02565, Jun 2025) generates controllable geometry problems via symbolic deduction with knowledge-point difficulty mapping. MathMixup (arXiv:2601.17006, Jan 2026) introduces difficulty-controllable data synthesis with curriculum learning for text-only mathematical reasoning (Qwen2.5-7B achieves 52.6% across 7 benchmarks). VISTA (arXiv:2411.05423, NeurIPS 2024 Workshop) uses multi-agent LLM framework. BeyondBench (ICLR 2026) demonstrates contamination-resistant procedural generation (10^15 instances, text-only). No generator connects difficulty control to cross-modal IRT parameters.

**Multimodal reasoning analysis:** MathLens / 'What MLLMs Learn' (arXiv:2510.01719, Oct 2025) decomposes MLLM performance into Perception, Reasoning, and Integration via geometry probes; key finding: RL primarily improves perceptual grounding while SFT improves reflective reasoning, and remaining errors increasingly stem from multimodal-specific integration failures. MathVista (ICLR 2024) defines a 5×7×19 taxonomy; SOTA: o3 at 86.8%. MATH-Vision (NeurIPS 2024) provides 3,040 problems with error taxonomy (as reported: ~42% Reasoning, ~32% Vision Recognition, ~15% Knowledge, ~7% Misunderstood, ~3% Reject, ~1% Calculation); SOTA: Kimi K2.6 at 93.2% with Python tool use (Hyperstack blog), ~87.4% without (BenchLM). SolidGeo (arXiv:2505.21177, May 2025) provides 3,113 3D problems. VCBench (arXiv:2504.18589, Apr 2025) emphasizes explicit visual dependency. The PAR survey (arXiv:2603.08291, ACL 2026) organizes the field into Perception, Alignment, and Reasoning, identifying their integration as an open challenge.

**Gap synthesis:** The field has independently solved modality-decomposed rewards (MoCA, PDCR, Perception-R1, CogFlow, PEARL), capability staging ('From Seeing to Thinking,' Infi-MMR), text-only IRT-guided training (PUDF, RIDE), difficulty-aware RL optimization (MathForge's DGPO, AdaRFT, GRPO-LEAD), multi-dimensional heuristic curriculum (VideoCuRL), verifiable data synthesis for visual reasoning RL (SynthRL), and diagnostic loops (DPE, DPPO). VideoCuRL demonstrates that orthogonal difficulty decomposition outperforms scalar scheduling, but uses training-free heuristic proxies without formal uncertainty quantification, data generation, or reward calibration. No work integrates cross-modal IRT decomposition with curriculum scheduling, targeted data generation, AND modality-aware training into a closed loop with principled parameter stability guarantees and graceful degradation.",
  "inspired_by": "User requirement: 'Multi-Modal Mathematical Reasoning — Integrating Visual, Symbolic, and Textual Understanding.' Untried synthesis: 'M3IRT's cross-modal 2PL IRT decomposition (evaluation tool) + proven modality-decomposed rewards (MoCA/PDCR/CogFlow/PEARL) + curriculum RL (VL-Cogito/E2H/Infi-MMR/VideoCuRL's orthogonal decomposition principle) + difficulty-aware RL optimization (MathForge's DGPO) + procedural visual math generation (DynaMath/MAVIS/SynthRL) + stable Bayesian IRT estimation (PUDF's Artificial Crowds + hierarchical priors) → a closed-loop training method that uses psychometric diagnosis to guide both curriculum scheduling and data generation, with confidence-aware fallback ensuring robustness.' Innovation pattern: 'Cross-Modal IRT Diagnosis → IRT-Parameterized Generation → Fisher-Information Curriculum Scheduling with Confidence Gating → Re-Diagnosis Loop.' VideoCuRL validates multi-axis difficulty decomposition; MathPrism provides the IRT-grounded instantiation with generation and reward calibration.",
  "approach": "We propose MathPrism, a training methodology for visual mathematical reasoning that bridges the gap between cross-modal psychometric evaluation and curriculum reinforcement learning. The key insight: M3IRT shows that VLM abilities decompose into modality-specific components, but this diagnostic power has never been connected to training data selection or curriculum scheduling — even as modality-decomposed rewards (MoCA, PDCR, Perception-R1, CogFlow, PEARL) and staged training (Infi-MMR, 'From Seeing to Thinking') have matured. VideoCuRL demonstrates that orthogonal difficulty decomposition outperforms single-axis curricula for video RL (ablation: −1.5% to −3.1% when either axis is removed), validating the multi-dimensional principle, but uses heuristic proxies (optical flow, keyframe entropy, Calibrated Surprisal) that lack calibrated uncertainty and serve as 'probabilistic guides' with high within-bin variance. CogFlow tells the model to first perceive correctly then reason correctly via quality gating, PEARL gates reasoning updates on perception checklist fidelity, and MoCA tells the model HOW to learn (route credit to perception vs reasoning errors), but none tells the model WHAT to learn next (which problems at which difficulty along which modality axis). MathForge demonstrates that difficulty-aware advantage normalization improves RL training, but uses scalar empirical accuracy — not multidimensional IRT profiling. MathPrism contributes the complementary piece: IRT-guided curriculum and generation that determine WHAT to train on, with robust estimation guarantees, formal uncertainty quantification, and graceful degradation — the IRT-grounded instantiation of multi-dimensional difficulty scheduling that VideoCuRL motivates with heuristics.

**Component 1 — Cross-Modal IRT Profiler.** Given a target VLM, we evaluate it on a diagnostic item bank (~2K problems drawn from MathVista, MATH-Vision, and DynaMath variants spanning the MathVista taxonomy). We fit M3IRT's multidimensional 2PL model to obtain the VLM's modality-specific ability profile: θ = (θ_base, θ_img, θ_txt, θ_cross). Critically, we also estimate item-level difficulty parameters b = (b_base, b_img, b_txt, b_cross) and discrimination parameters a for all problems in our generation bank. Unlike PUDF's 1PL Rasch model (which treats all items as equally discriminative, varying only in scalar difficulty) and RIDE's 1PL difficulty ranker (which produces a single difficulty score for question rewriting reward), our profiler captures the multidimensional structure of multimodal difficulty — the same problem can be easy visually but hard for cross-modal integration. Unlike VideoCuRL's heuristic proxies (optical flow, keyframe entropy, Calibrated Surprisal), which provide ordinal difficulty rankings without calibrated confidence, IRT provides calibrated continuous-valued latent traits with posterior uncertainty estimates, enabling both fine-grained curriculum control and principled fallback when estimates are unreliable. Unlike 'From Seeing to Thinking''s computational filter (which only checks whether models fail with images but succeed with captions), IRT provides calibrated continuous-valued latent traits enabling fine-grained curriculum control. Unlike CogFlow's fixed threshold τ for Visual-Gated Policy Optimization (which provides binary quality filtering without difficulty characterization) and PEARL's binary pass/fail perception checklists, IRT provides continuous multi-dimensional difficulty profiles that enable graduated curriculum control.

*IRT Parameter Stability and Robust Estimation.* A central technical challenge is IRT parameter stability: standard 2PL MLE requires ~500 respondents for stable item parameter estimates, but the pool of available VLMs is inherently small. We address this via three complementary mechanisms:

(a) *Augmented Calibration Panel with Practical Assembly Strategy*: Inspired by PUDF's Artificial Crowds approach (which constructs 60 effective respondents from 13 models × 5 epoch checkpoints for stable 1PL calibration), we assemble our panel from three sources with varying checkpoint availability:

*Source 1 — Families with released stage-wise checkpoints*: InternVL3/3.5 releases checkpoints at each training stage (CPT, SFT, MPO, CascadeRL) at multiple scales (1B, 4B, 8B, 14B, 38B), providing 15–20 variants directly. LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 releases stage0 (post-alignment), Base, and Instruct checkpoints at 8B scale, providing 3 variants. These publicly available intermediate checkpoints are the primary source, requiring only evaluation cost (~80 A100-hrs for diagnostic bank evaluation).

*Source 2 — Families requiring checkpoint generation*: For families that release only final checkpoints (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL at 3B/7B/72B, Phi-Vision), we generate diversity via lightweight LoRA fine-tuning on a small held-out math dataset (~5K problems) with 3–5 different configurations (varying learning rate, LoRA rank, training epochs). Each LoRA variant produces a distinct ability profile while sharing the same base architecture. Cost: ~30 A100-hrs total for LoRA fine-tuning across all variants (~2 hrs per LoRA configuration per model).

*Source 3 — Scale diversity*: Different parameter scales of the same architecture (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-3B vs -7B vs -72B, InternVL3.5-1B vs -8B vs -14B) naturally provide distinct ability profiles and are already publicly available.

This strategy yields 60–100 effective respondents: ~20 from InternVL stage checkpoints, ~3 from LLaVA-OV stages, ~12–15 from Qwen/Phi LoRA variants, ~8–10 from scale-diverse final checkpoints, plus additional variants from other open VLM families (e.g., Cambrian, Idefics). The IRT literature on parameter estimation with hierarchical models demonstrates that this range is sufficient for stable 2PL estimation when combined with Bayesian methods.

(b) *Hierarchical Bayesian 2PL Estimation*: Rather than standard MLE, we employ a hierarchical Bayesian formulation: discrimination parameters a_{i,d} ~ LogNormal(μ_a, σ_a) with μ_a calibrated from pilot data, difficulty parameters b_{i,d} ~ Normal(μ_b, σ_b) with hierarchical priors on (μ_b, σ_b). The optimized hierarchical 2PL (OH2PL) developed by König, Spoden, and Frey (2020, Applied Psychological Measurement) demonstrates that hierarchical Bayesian 2PL with optimized hyperpriors (half-Cauchy and Exponential distributions for variance components, reparametrization to streamline sampling) produces unbiased discrimination parameter estimates even at N=50 respondents, compared to substantial bias with MLE at the same sample size. Their robustness study (König, Spoden & Frey, 2022, Behavior Research Methods) confirms these findings hold across varying variance component magnitudes, item parameter correlations (0 to .3), and hyperprior specifications, with bias largely independent of specification at N≥100. We implement estimation via variational inference (NumPyro) for scalability, with posterior variance on each parameter providing built-in uncertainty quantification.

(c) *Warm-Start Sequential Re-Diagnosis*: During iterative re-diagnosis (every K training steps), we initialize from the previous posterior rather than re-estimating from scratch. This Bayesian updating approach reduces estimation variance and provides natural regularization against parameter drift. We implement item parameter drift detection: items where the posterior shift between consecutive calibrations exceeds 2 posterior standard deviations are flagged, and either re-anchored using stable anchor items or excluded from curriculum guidance. This parallels established item parameter drift methodology from computerized adaptive testing.

The calibration panel is assembled once (requiring ~110 A100-hrs: ~80 for evaluation + ~30 for LoRA variant generation) and updated incrementally via warm-start re-diagnosis.

**Component 2 — Modality-Targeted Problem Generator.** We extend the DynaMath/MAVIS paradigm with IRT-parameterized difficulty control. Building on MathMixup's demonstration that difficulty-controllable synthesis improves mathematical reasoning (text-only), MathForge's Multi-Aspect Question Reformulation (which reformulates along background/term/sub-problem axes), and SynthRL's verifiable data synthesis for visual reasoning RL (which uses LLM rewriting for holistic difficulty augmentation with two-criterion verification), we introduce the first multimodal generator with cross-modal difficulty dials parameterized by IRT. SynthRL demonstrates that synthesized harder visual math problems improve RL training (+1.0% avg across 5 benchmarks), but treats difficulty holistically — the same augmentation cannot independently target visual vs. textual vs. cross-modal weaknesses. Our contribution is modality-decomposed, IRT-parameterized difficulty control. For each covered MathVista taxonomy cell, parameterized Python generators produce question-image-answer triples with difficulty controls along each modality dimension: (a) Image difficulty: diagram complexity, label density, visual noise, resolution degradation — targeting Vision Recognition errors (~32% of MATH-Vision error taxonomy); (b) Text difficulty: linguistic complexity, multi-step chain length, irrelevant information — targeting Reasoning errors (~42%); (c) Cross-modal difficulty: degree of text-image interdependence, implicit vs. explicit visual references, information split between modalities — targeting Integration errors identified by MathLens. Given the IRT profiler's diagnosis, the generator produces training batches where difficulty is concentrated in the weak modality dimension while other dimensions remain at the model's comfort zone. We re-parameterize DynaMath's 501 existing programs with modality dials and author ~15 new generators for high-priority uncovered taxonomy cells. SDE-GPG's symbolic deduction engine is adapted for geometry cells. Verification follows SynthRL's two-criterion approach: generated problems must be solvable (≥4/16 rollouts pass) and IRT difficulty estimates must fall within the target range for each modality dimension.

**Component 3 — IRT-Guided Curriculum RL (IRT-CuRL).** We train the target VLM using GRPO with four innovations:

(a) *Multi-dimensional IRT curriculum scheduling with confidence-aware fallback*: Instead of a single easy→hard progression (VL-Cogito, E2H Reasoner), capability-type staging ('From Seeing to Thinking'), predetermined phase transitions (Infi-MMR), scalar difficulty balancing (MathForge's DGPO), reward-signal-based adaptive difficulty (AdaRFT), or heuristic multi-axis scheduling (VideoCuRL's Diagonal Wavefront with optical flow/entropy/surprisal proxies), we maintain IRT-parameterized difficulty trajectories along each modality dimension simultaneously. VideoCuRL's ablation confirms multi-axis superiority (−1.5% to −3.1% with single-axis), and SPEED-RL's theoretical analysis (though the paper was withdrawn) supports the intuition that intermediate-difficulty selection maximizes gradient signal-to-noise — our Fisher-information criterion provides a principled, IRT-grounded formalization of this insight. As 'From Seeing to Thinking' demonstrated, capability-type staging and difficulty-based curricula are orthogonal and complementary (combining both yielded their best results at 62.99%). # Paper Analysis: Difficulty-Aware Group Normalization for Multimodal LLMs

## Core Details

**Title:** Enhancing Multi-Modal LLMs Reasoning via Difficulty-Aware Group Normalization

**Authors:** Jinghan Li, Junfeng Fang, Jinda Lu, Yuan Wang, Xiaoyan Guo, Tianyu Zhang, Xiang Wang, Xiangnan He

**Method Name:** Durian (Difficulty-aware group normalization)

---

## Technical Approach

The method addresses a fundamental problem in extending reinforcement learning techniques (RLVR and GRPO) to multimodal settings. The authors identify that standard deviation-based normalization becomes unstable when samples have extreme reward values, which impacts multimodal models particularly severely.

**Difficulty Characterization:** The framework measures sample difficulty through two dimensions:
- **Perceptual complexity:** Quantified using visual entropy analysis
- **Reasoning uncertainty:** Captured by model confidence scores

**Implementation Strategy:** Rather than applying uniform normalization across all samples, Durian groups samples by their difficulty levels and calculates standard deviation independently within each group. This preserves the model's ability to distinguish between samples of similar difficulty while eliminating sensitivity to outlier cases with near-extreme rewards.

---

## Key Results & Differentiation

The paper reports "significant performance gains across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks" through this approach. The critical distinction is that Durian maintains intra-group differentiation (GRPO's strength) while preventing extreme samples from distorting the normalization process—a challenge unique to multimodal architectures where both visual and reasoning errors compound.

The abstract does not reference Item Response Theory (IRT)-based approaches, so direct differentiation from IRT methods cannot be established from this document.

## Title & Authors
**Full Title:** "VADE: Variance-Aware Dynamic Sampling via Online Sample-Level Difficulty Estimation for Multimodal RL"

**Authors:** Zengjie Hu, Jiantao Qiu, Tianyi Bai, Haojin Yang, Binhang Yuan, Qi Jing, Conghui He, Wentao Zhang

**arXiv ID:** 2511.18902 (Submitted: November 24, 2025)

## Method Overview
VADE addresses the gradient vanishing problem in group-based policy optimization methods (GRPO, GSPO) by implementing dynamic sample selection. The framework operates through three integrated components:

1. **Online Difficulty Estimation:** Uses Beta distributions to estimate sample-level difficulty in real-time
2. **Thompson Sampling:** Maximizes information gain by leveraging estimated correctness probability
3. **Two-Scale Prior Decay:** Maintains robust estimation as policies evolve during training

## Key Distinguishing Features
Rather than relying on static filtering criteria or prior dataset knowledge, VADE provides "real-time adaptability" through continuous difficulty assessment. The approach proactively selects informative samples before rollout generation, eliminating computational overhead associated with post-hoc filtering methods.

## Results & Impact
According to the abstract, VADE demonstrates:
- Consistent outperformance over baseline methods on multimodal reasoning benchmarks
- Enhanced sample efficiency
- "Dramatic reduction in computational overhead"
- Plug-and-play compatibility with existing group-based RL algorithms

Code and models are available through the project website.

The main challenge is the instability of std-based normalization, which is easily distorted by extreme samples with nearly positive or negative rewards, and multimodal models are particularly sensitive to such distortions, as both perceptual and reasoning errors influence their responses.

# PERM Technical Summary

## (1) IRT Model Specification
PERM uses the **continuous 1-Parameter Logistic (1PL) model**, also called the Rasch model. Difficulty is **scalar-valued** (d ∈ ℝⁿ represents a latent continuous dimension), not multidimensional item response theory (mIRT). The model uses: "the continuous distribution of a standard normal" to relate ability (a) and difficulty (d) through the relation a−d.

## (2) Environment Difficulty Parameterization
In the Jumper domain, difficulty is controlled via two environment parameters:
- **Spike density**: probability scalar [0.0, 1.0] controlling spike frequency
- **Height variance**: 4-element probability vector controlling terrain elevation distribution

The framework assumes difficulty d ∝ 1/r (inverse proportional to reward), allowing "environment parameters λ as an item which the student agent...responds to."

## (3) Zone of Proximal Development Implementation
The core ZPD mechanism: "optimal learning takes place when the difficulty of the environment matches the ability of the student." When a=d, the probability of achieving normalized average score r=0 equals 0.5, representing "equal probability of the student overperforming or underperforming." The curriculum sets d_{t+1} = a_t at each step.

## (4) Domains/Environments
**Only Jumper** (proprietary 2D obstacle course game built in Unity). The authors acknowledge this limitation: "simplicity of the Jumper domain...led to a ceiling effect in level difficulties."

## (5) Key Quantitative Results

**RL agents**: PERM-trained agents completed more levels and traversed deeper despite training under higher difficulty.

**Human subjects** (N=230):
- PERM participants required **5.8 attempts** vs 7.17 (random) and 8.225 (no training) on final test (p<0.01)
- **74.7% completion rate** for PERM vs 63.0% random (χ²=9.24, p<0.01)
- Spent **61.02 seconds** per attempt vs 45.01 (random)

## (6) IRT-RL Connection
Two-stage process: 
- **Stage 1**: RL agents train with domain randomization; PERM learns from 14,506 environment-agent interactions
- **Stage 2**: Pre-trained PERM deployed as teacher (no real-time RL updates), enabling "offline training" across different students

PERM uses variational inference (VIBO framework) to learn latent representations, then adds a decoder generating λ conditioned on desired difficulty d.

## (7) Vision/Multimodal Connection
**None identified**. The paper focuses purely on reward-based curriculum generation with no mention of visual features or multimodal approaches.

# Durian: Difficulty-Aware Group Normalization - Technical Details

## 1. Perceptual Complexity Measurement

Durian measures visual complexity through spectral analysis of image patch features:

- **Process**: Extracts patch-level features from the visual encoder, computing an empirical covariance matrix across patches
- **Eigenvalue decomposition**: Performs spectral analysis on the symmetric covariance matrix to obtain eigenvalues
- **Entropy calculation**: Computes Shannon entropy of the normalized eigenvalue distribution: "high entropy indicates a more diverse distribution of visual features, implying a richer and more complex visual structure"
- **Interpretation**: Low entropy = concentrated variance (easy), high entropy = distributed variance across dimensions (difficult)

## 2. Reasoning Uncertainty via Model Confidence

Measures confidence through token and sequence-level probabilities:

- **Token-level**: Uses "token-level log probabilities" from the language model
- **Sequence aggregation**: "the sequence-level log probability for response os,i is L_{s,i} = ∑ π_θ(o^n|...)"
- **Final metric**: Average log probability across G rollouts: "High and consistent L(Q_s) indicates reliable reasoning chains, whereas low or fluctuating L(Q_s) reflects epistemic uncertainty"

## 3. Difficulty-Based Regrouping

Creates separate groups for each difficulty dimension:

**Perceptual regrouping**: Uses 25th and 75th percentiles to partition into three groups (easy, medium, hard); each group shares its own standard deviation for normalization

**Reasoning regrouping**: Divides samples into b quantile-based groups by confidence scores; "Within each group, samples share the same std during advantage calculation"

**Combination**: Element-wise weighted sum: "A^Combined = α_Ori·A^GRPO + α_Percep·A^Perceptual + α_Reason·A^Reasoning"

## 4. Benchmark Results

**Evaluation metrics**: Accuracy (%) on 5 benchmarks with Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model

**Key results using 2.1K training samples (Geometry3K)**:
- MathVerse: 52.8% (vs. 46.2% baseline)
- MathVision: 28.8% (vs. 25.0%)
- MathVista: 72.3% (vs. 67.5%)
- WeMath: 69.2% (vs. 63.1%)
- HallusionBench: 72.9% (vs. 64.6%)

**Average improvement**: "more than 11.3% average performance improvements" over baseline

On larger ViRL39K dataset: 60.1% average accuracy

## 5. Base Models

- **Primary**: Qwen2.5-VL-7B with visual encoder from same architecture
- **Framework**: EasyR1 reinforcement learning framework
- **Hardware**: 8 NVIDIA H20 96G GPUs
- **Rollout configuration**: Rollout size of 8, global batch size 128

## 6. Distinction from Similar Approaches

The paper does not explicitly compare with "MathForge's DGPO" in the provided content. However, Durian's innovation centers on: decomposing difficulty into explicit perceptual (data-centric) and reasoning (model-centric) dimensions, then sharing variance statistics within each difficulty group rather than computing across all samples uniformly—directly addressing "sensitivity to extreme samples" inherent in standard GRPO.

# VADE Framework: Key Technical Details

## (1) Beta Distribution for Difficulty Modeling

The framework maintains parameters (αᵢ, βᵢ) for each sample, where these represent cumulative counts of correct and incorrect responses. The correctness probability pᵢ follows a Beta distribution: "Beta(αᵢ+1,βᵢ+1)" for numerical stability. When a sample generates G rollouts with rᵢ correct answers, the posterior becomes "Beta(αᵢ+1+rᵢ,βᵢ+1+G−rᵢ)".

## (2) Thompson Sampling Strategy

The method samples a candidate probability p̃ᵢ from the posterior distribution, then computes information gain as "ℐ̃ᵢ(θt) = p̃ᵢ(1−p̃ᵢ)²". The framework "select[s] the top-B data points with the highest ℐ̃ᵢ" for each training batch, balancing exploration through uncertainty with exploitation of high-utility samples.

## (3) Two-Scale Prior Decay

Two decay parameters (λ₁ ≪ λ₂) handle different scenarios:
- **Selected samples**: αᵢ,ₜ ← λ₁αᵢ,ₜ₋₁ + rₜ (λ₁=0.2, aggressive decay for distribution shift)
- **Unselected samples**: αᵢ,ₜ ← λ₂αᵢ,ₜ₋₁ (λ₂=0.999, gradual decay for generalization effects)

## (4) Benchmark Results

Training on Qwen2.5-VL-7B across five benchmarks shows:
- **vs. vanilla GRPO**: +2.93% average improvement
- **vs. DAPO**: "VADE attain[s] 99.5% of DAPO's peak performance while using nearly three times fewer rollout inferences"
- Specific gains include MathVista (75.10), MathVerse (45.65), ScienceQA (91.67)

## (5) Base Models

Experiments used "Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct models" across both GRPO and GSPO algorithms.

## (6) GRPO Baseline Comparison

With Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, vanilla GRPO achieved 72.85 average score; VADE reached 75.10—a 2.25-point absolute improvement in this setup.

## Overview

The proposed competence-aware curriculum for visual concept learning in a question-answering manner includes a neural-symbolic concept learner for learning the visual concepts and a multi-dimensional Item Response Theory (mIRT) model for guiding the learning process with an adaptive curriculum.

The mIRT effectively estimates the concept difficulty and the model competence at each learning step from accumulated model responses. The approach utilizes multi-dimensional Item Response Theory (mIRT) to estimate the concept difficulty and model competence at each learning step from accumulated model responses. Item Response Theory (IRT) is a widely adopted method in psychometrics that estimates the human ability and the item difficulty from human responses on various items. # VPPO Technical Details

## (1) Token-Level Visual Dependency Computation

Token visual dependency is quantified using KL divergence between policy distributions conditioned on the original image versus a perturbed version:

**Definition**: "the KL divergence between the policy's output distributions conditioned on I and I′" where I′ is "a non-informative, perturbed version."

The metric captures how much the visual input changes the model's token prediction distribution at each step.

## (2) Trajectory-Level Advantage Reweighting

Trajectory dependency is calculated as the mean of token-level scores across the full sequence. A shaping factor rescales the original advantage:

α(τᵢ) = βₘᵢₙ + (βₘₐₓ - βₘᵢₙ) × normalized_dependency_score

The shaped advantage becomes: Â′(τᵢ) = α(τᵢ) · Â_GRPO(τᵢ). This "adaptively amplifies updates for trajectories with high visual engagement."

## (3) Sparse Gradient Mask for Top-k% Tokens

A binary mask identifies the top k% of tokens with highest visual dependency scores:

mᵢ,ₜ = 1 if token t is in the top-k% set, 0 otherwise

"Policy gradients are computed only for the pivotal tokens that bridge vision and language, effectively filtering out noise from generic tokens."

**Component 1 — Cross-Modal IRT Profiler.** Given a target VLM, we evaluate it on a diagnostic item bank (~2K problems drawn from MathVista, MATH-Vision, and DynaMath variants spanning the MathVista taxonomy). We fit M3IRT's multidimensional 2PL model to obtain the VLM's modality-specific ability profile: θ = (θ_base, θ_img, θ_txt, θ_cross). Critically, we also estimate item-level difficulty parameters b = (b_base, b_img, b_txt, b_cross) and discrimination parameters a for all problems in our generation bank. Unlike PUDF's 1PL Rasch model (which treats all items as equally discriminative, varying only in scalar difficulty), RIDE's 1PL difficulty ranker (which produces a single difficulty score for question rewriting reward), and PERM's scalar 1PL difficulty-to-environment mapping, our profiler captures the multidimensional structure of multimodal difficulty — the same problem can be easy visually but hard for cross-modal integration. Unlike Li et al.'s mIRT (whose dimensions track concept-type competence within CLEVR's structured ontology), our cross-modal 2PL IRT decomposes ability along modality axes relevant to modern VLM mathematical reasoning — capturing whether failures stem from visual perception, textual reasoning, or their integration. Unlike VideoCuRL's heuristic proxies (optical flow, keyframe entropy, Calibrated Surprisal), which provide ordinal difficulty rankings without calibrated confidence, IRT provides calibrated continuous-valued latent traits with posterior uncertainty estimates, enabling both fine-grained curriculum control and principled fallback when estimates are unreliable. Unlike Durian's visual entropy and model confidence (which characterize individual samples without population-level calibration) and VADE's Beta-distribution online difficulty estimates (which track per-sample correctness probability without modality decomposition), IRT provides population-level psychometric profiling with modality-specific decomposition. Unlike 'From Seeing to Thinking''s computational filter (which only checks whether models fail with images but succeed with captions), IRT provides calibrated continuous-valued latent traits enabling fine-grained curriculum control. Unlike CogFlow's fixed threshold τ for Visual-Gated Policy Optimization (which provides binary quality filtering without difficulty characterization), PEARL's binary pass/fail perception checklists, and VPPO's token-level KL divergence (which measures visual dependency per token without difficulty characterization), IRT provides continuous multi-dimensional difficulty profiles that enable graduated curriculum control.

*IRT Parameter Stability and Robust Estimation.* A central technical challenge is IRT parameter stability: standard 2PL MLE requires ~500 respondents for stable item parameter estimates, but the pool of available VLMs is inherently small. We address this via three complementary mechanisms:

(a) *Augmented Calibration Panel with Practical Assembly Strategy*: Inspired by PUDF's Artificial Crowds approach (which constructs 60 effective respondents from 13 models × 5 epoch checkpoints for stable 1PL calibration), we assemble our panel from three sources with varying checkpoint availability:

*Source 1 — Families with released stage-wise checkpoints*: InternVL3/3.5 releases checkpoints at each training stage (CPT, SFT, MPO, CascadeRL) at multiple scales (1B, 4B, 8B, 14B, 38B), providing 15–20 variants directly. LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 releases stage0 (post-alignment), Base, and Instruct checkpoints at 8B scale, providing 3 variants. These publicly available intermediate checkpoints are the primary source, requiring only evaluation cost (~80 A100-hrs for diagnostic bank evaluation).

*Source 2 — Families requiring checkpoint generation*: For families that release only final checkpoints (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL at 3B/7B/72B, Phi-Vision), we generate diversity via lightweight LoRA fine-tuning on a small held-out math dataset (~5K problems) with 3–5 different configurations (varying learning rate, LoRA rank, training epochs). Each LoRA variant produces a distinct ability profile while sharing the same base architecture. Cost: ~30 A100-hrs total for LoRA fine-tuning across all variants (~2 hrs per LoRA configuration per model).

*Source 3 — Scale diversity*: Different parameter scales of the same architecture (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-3B vs -7B vs -72B, InternVL3.5-1B vs -8B vs -14B) naturally provide distinct ability profiles and are already publicly available.

This strategy yields 60–100 effective respondents: ~20 from InternVL stage checkpoints, ~3 from LLaVA-OV stages, ~12–15 from Qwen/Phi LoRA variants, ~8–10 from scale-diverse final checkpoints, plus additional variants from other open VLM families (e.g., Cambrian, Idefics). The IRT literature on parameter estimation with hierarchical models demonstrates that this range is sufficient for stable 2PL estimation when combined with Bayesian methods.

(b) *Hierarchical Bayesian 2PL Estimation*: Rather than standard MLE, we employ a hierarchical Bayesian formulation: discrimination parameters a_{i,d} ~ LogNormal(μ_a, σ_a) with μ_a calibrated from pilot data, difficulty parameters b_{i,d} ~ Normal(μ_b, σ_b) with hierarchical priors on (μ_b, σ_b). The optimized hierarchical 2PL (OH2PL) developed by König, Spoden, and Frey (2020, Applied Psychological Measurement) demonstrates that hierarchical Bayesian 2PL with optimized hyperpriors (half-Cauchy and Exponential distributions for variance components, reparametrization to streamline sampling) produces unbiased discrimination parameter estimates even at N=50 respondents, compared to substantial bias with MLE at the same sample size. Their robustness study (König, Spoden & Frey, 2022, Behavior Research Methods) confirms these findings hold across varying variance component magnitudes, item parameter correlations (0 to .3), and hyperprior specifications, with bias largely independent of specification at N≥100. We implement estimation via variational inference (NumPyro) for scalability, with posterior variance on each parameter providing built-in uncertainty quantification.

(c) *Warm-Start Sequential Re-Diagnosis*: During iterative re-diagnosis (every K training steps), we initialize from the previous posterior rather than re-estimating from scratch. This Bayesian updating approach reduces estimation variance and provides natural regularization against parameter drift. We implement item parameter drift detection: items where the posterior shift between consecutive calibrations exceeds 2 posterior standard deviations are flagged, and either re-anchored using stable anchor items or excluded from curriculum guidance. This parallels established item parameter drift methodology from computerized adaptive testing.

The calibration panel is assembled once (requiring ~110 A100-hrs: ~80 for evaluation + ~30 for LoRA variant generation) and updated incrementally via warm-start re-diagnosis.

**Component 2 — Modality-Targeted Problem Generator.** We extend the DynaMath/MAVIS paradigm with IRT-parameterized difficulty control. Building on MathMixup's demonstration that difficulty-controllable synthesis improves mathematical reasoning (text-only), MathForge's Multi-Aspect Question Reformulation (which reformulates along background/term/sub-problem axes), and SynthRL's verifiable data synthesis for visual reasoning RL (which uses LLM rewriting for holistic difficulty augmentation with two-criterion verification), we introduce the first multimodal generator with cross-modal difficulty dials parameterized by IRT. SynthRL demonstrates that synthesized harder visual math problems improve RL training (+1.0% avg across 5 benchmarks), but treats difficulty holistically — the same augmentation cannot independently target visual vs. textual vs. cross-modal weaknesses. Our contribution is modality-decomposed, IRT-parameterized difficulty control. For each covered MathVista taxonomy cell, parameterized Python generators produce question-image-answer triples with difficulty controls along each modality dimension: (a) Image difficulty: diagram complexity, label density, visual noise, resolution degradation — targeting Vision Recognition errors (~32% of MATH-Vision error taxonomy); (b) Text difficulty: linguistic complexity, multi-step chain length, irrelevant information — targeting Reasoning errors (~42%); (c) Cross-modal difficulty: degree of text-image interdependence, implicit vs. explicit visual references, information split between modalities — targeting Integration errors identified by MathLens. Given the IRT profiler's diagnosis, the generator produces training batches where difficulty is concentrated in the weak modality dimension while other dimensions remain at the model's comfort zone. We re-parameterize DynaMath's 501 existing programs with modality dials and author ~15 new generators for high-priority uncovered taxonomy cells. SDE-GPG's symbolic deduction engine is adapted for geometry cells. Verification follows SynthRL's two-criterion approach: generated problems must be solvable (≥4/16 rollouts pass) and IRT difficulty estimates must fall within the target range for each modality dimension.

**Component 3 — IRT-Guided Curriculum RL (IRT-CuRL).** We train the target VLM using GRPO with four innovations:

(a) *Multi-dimensional IRT curriculum scheduling with confidence-aware fallback*: Instead of a single easy→hard progression (VL-Cogito, E2H Reasoner), capability-type staging ('From Seeing to Thinking', RewardMap), predetermined phase transitions (Infi-MMR), scalar difficulty balancing (MathForge's DGPO), reward-signal-based adaptive difficulty (AdaRFT), heuristic multi-axis scheduling (VideoCuRL's Diagonal Wavefront with optical flow/entropy/surprisal proxies), or heuristic difficulty-based normalization (Durian's visual entropy + model confidence grouping), we maintain IRT-parameterized difficulty trajectories along each modality dimension simultaneously. VideoCuRL's ablation confirms multi-axis superiority (−1.5% to −3.1% with single-axis), and SPEED-RL's theoretical analysis (though the paper was withdrawn) supports the intuition that intermediate-difficulty selection maximizes gradient signal-to-noise — our Fisher-information criterion provides a principled, IRT-grounded formalization of this insight. Li et al.'s 40% data reduction and 3× convergence speedup on CLEVR demonstrates the concrete efficiency gains achievable with mIRT-guided curriculum over heuristic alternatives. PERM's ZPD-based curriculum (d_{t+1} = a_t) provides a scalar precedent that our Fisher-information-guided multi-dimensional scheduling generalizes. As 'From Seeing to Thinking' demonstrated, capability-type staging and difficulty-based curricula are orthogonal and complementary (combining both yielded their best results at 62.99%). MathPrism contributes the IRT-parameterized difficulty dimension: at training step t, we sample problems whose IRT difficulty profile b*(t) maximizes expected Fisher information I(θ(t), b) along the weakest modality dimension — adapting ATLAS's item-selection criterion from adaptive testing to adaptive training. This provides principled, continuous difficulty control with formal uncertainty rather than heuristic proxies (VL-Cogito's accuracy-based weighting, VCRL's reward variance, VideoCuRL's optical flow/entropy/surprisal, AdaRFT's reward-signal adjustment, Durian's visual entropy/model confidence, VADE's Beta-distribution correctness probability, 'Revisiting Data Sampling''s PISM/CMAB attention patterns, 'Unlocking Difficulty Prior''s empirical group accuracy, MathForge's negative mean accuracy). The scheduling is compatible with capability staging: if desired, perception-focused problems can precede reasoning-focused ones, with IRT controlling difficulty within each stage.

*Confidence-aware scheduling*: Because IRT parameter estimates carry uncertainty (captured by posterior variance in our Bayesian formulation) — a limitation that heuristic proxies like VideoCuRL's, Durian's, and VADE's cannot even quantify in psychometric terms — we implement confidence-gated Fisher information guidance.
